Where it began

Daren Sammy was born on 20 December 1983 in Micoud Quarter, St Lucia. He first played senior cricket at 17, and in 2002 he went to New Zealand with the West Indies Under-19 World Cup side, alongside future senior players such as Dwayne Bravo and Lendl Simmons.

His first West Indies cap came in odd fashion. In June 2004 he was named for a one-day game with New Zealand at the Rose Bowl that rain wiped out before a ball was bowled, but the toss had taken place, so it counted. Later that year, aged 20, he played for real against Bangladesh and became the first international cricketer from St Lucia. West Indies went on to win that Champions Trophy.

The player

His Test debut, against England at Old Trafford in June 2007, was a startling one. He took 7 for 66, with three wickets in five balls, the best debut figures by a West Indian since Alf Valentine in 1950. In 38 Tests between 2007 and 2013 he took 84 wickets at 35.80, with four five-wicket innings, and scored 1,323 runs at 21.69 with a hundred and five fifties.

In October 2010 he was made Test captain, and he led West Indies in 30 Tests: 8 won, 12 lost and 10 drawn. In 2011 his seven wickets against Pakistan ended a run of 17 Tests without a West Indies win. In 2012 in England he made 106, his only Test hundred, from number eight. He also captained West Indies to the World Twenty20 title in 2012, beating Sri Lanka in the final, and again in 2016, beating England, the first captain to win it twice.

What made him special

Sammy saw himself as the team's workhorse. He bowled long, tight spells, building pressure with dot balls, and felt batsmen relaxed against a support bowler and made mistakes. With the bat he liked to hurry. In a one-day international against South Africa in Antigua he reached fifty in 20 balls, at the time the fastest by a West Indian.

He never moved the ball a great deal, and a Test batting average just under 22 says he was more often useful than decisive. But he knew when to deliver. After a quiet 2012 World Twenty20, he saved his best for the final: an unbeaten 26 off 15 balls, plus two important wickets.

Away from the middle

He was made an OBE in 2017. For his part in bringing international cricket back to Pakistan he received the Nishan-e-Pakistan in 2020, along with honorary Pakistani citizenship; he had captained Peshawar Zalmi to the title in the Pakistan Super League's second season and later coached them. In May 2023 he became head coach of West Indies in limited-overs cricket. His foundation gives scholarships to young people.

And finally

In 2016 the Beausejour Cricket Ground near Gros Islet was renamed in his honour. Few cricketers have begun with a match in which not a ball was bowled and ended up with a stadium carrying their name.
